title: Myth of Extinction and Native Survivance
summary: Older claims that Long Island Native people no longer existed are misleading; Native communities maintained identity, kinship, culture, political action, and public presence into the present.
content:
Many older histories described Long Island Native people as if they had vanished. That language is inaccurate and harmful because it confuses land loss, intermarriage, relocation, and colonial pressure with disappearance.

Native people on Long Island continued to live in families, churches, neighborhoods, reservations, public gatherings, labor networks, and cultural organizations. Shinnecock, Unkechaug, Montaukett, Matinecock, Setalcott, and other communities maintained identity and relationships even when outsiders denied or misunderstood them.

This topic helps readers interpret monuments, newspapers, court decisions, and local histories that used last-of-the-tribe language. Public interpretation should explain those claims as colonial-era and later myths, not as facts about Native survival.
